justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline across the three horizons, starting near 73.2 for the one-day forecast and nudging toward 74.0 over the month. This gradual drift likely reflects whatever underlying trend or mean-reversion dynamic was present in the data at the time of the forecast — in other words, the series appeared to have mild positive momentum or a slightly upward equilibrium, so absent new information, the most defensible central estimate was to carry that forward with a gentle slope. The one-day estimate is essentially anchored to the last observed value with minimal adjustment, while the one-week and one-month estimates allow for slightly more drift toward what might be a perceived fair value or trend target.

The confidence interval widths expand meaningfully as the horizon lengthens, which is a direct reflection of compounding uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 3.4 units, consistent with typical short-run volatility in a moderately stable series. By one week, that span grows to 7 units, and by one month it reaches 14 units, roughly doubling at each step. This scaling reflects the standard statistical intuition that uncertainty accumulates — shocks that occur over the intervening period can push the realized value progressively further from any point estimate made today. The widths also implicitly account for the possibility of regime changes or news-driven moves that are unpredictable in timing but plausible over longer windows.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the upside, a strongly positive macroeconomic surprise, a policy announcement, or a sentiment shift could produce a rapid jump well above 77 or even 81. On the downside, a risk-off episode, negative data release, or liquidity shock could push the value below 71.5 in the very near term or below 67 over the month. These tail events are by definition unlikely in any single period, but they represent the kinds of discontinuous moves that standard interval estimates based on historical volatility tend to understate. Fat tails in financial and economic data mean the true probability of extreme outcomes is generally higher than a normal-distribution assumption would suggest, so my stated 90% intervals should be understood as approximate rather than precise probabilistic guarantees.
